newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian Commodities Roundup - Sept 20.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian Commodities Roundup - Sept 20.

text.p: The copper price managed to extend a modest rally after sagging recently despite news on Thursday that Sumitomo Corp of Japan had raised estimates of its huge losses on trade in the metal.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index ended 0.75 points lower at 245.14 points.

Sumitomo said losses soared to $2.6 billion from $1.8 billion after it liquidated most of its uncovered positions and that it would seek prosecution of the trading star who it alleges ran up the losses in maverick deals, Yasuo Hamanaka.
But its statement still left the market unclear whether more selling may have to be done by banks that may have taken over the long Sumitomo position run by Hamanaka.
"It would be foolish to think that this marks the final chapter of the story," said Robin Bahr, an analyst with brokerage Brandeis in London.
After some volatility, however, London Metal Exchange three-months copper ended the afternoon kerb session up $11 per tonne at $1936. This compared with $1,850 during last week.
Copper had begun to rally late on Tuesday, led by buying and investment bank interest on New York's Comex futures market.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, grain prices were little changed at the weaker levels seen lately with Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) December wheat futures at $4.23 per bushel.
The easier values after the spike up to $7.50 earlier this year reflect bumper harvest that may begin to rebuild world grain stocks from current 20-year lows.
The European Union reintroduced subsidised grain exports on Thursday.

Gold was also little changed around $383 per ounce after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) decided to postpone a decison on whether to sell some of its gold to help poor Third World nations pay their debt.

It left bullion dealers uncertain about longer-term direction for the metal although firmer prices may be the immediate prospect. Buying tends to be stepped up around this time of year ahead of religious festivals in Asia and the West.
